reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / Scriver's OMMBID
clinicalPearls: Represents the milder, later-onset counterpart of I-cell disease within the same mannose-6-phosphate targeting pathway
Results from partial deficiency of GlcNAc-1-phosphotransferase, so lysosomal enzyme mistargeting is incomplete
Presents in mid-childhood with progressive joint stiffness, particularly of the shoulders and hands, and slowly progressive skeletal changes
Cognition is normal or only mildly affected, in contrast to the severe course of mucolipidosis II
Like I-cell disease, plasma lysosomal enzyme activities are elevated while intracellular activities are reduced
Two genetic forms exist: ML III alpha/beta from GNPTAB variants and ML III gamma from GNPTG variants
Hip dysplasia, aortic valve involvement, and mild corneal changes can develop over time
reference.pathophysiology: Pseudo-Hurler polydystrophy is caused by partial deficiency of UDP-N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase, the enzyme that generates the mannose-6-phosphate signal directing lysosomal hydrolases to the lysosome. Variants in GNPTAB (alpha/beta subunits, ML III alpha/beta) or GNPTG (gamma subunit, ML III gamma) leave greater residual phosphotransferase function than in mucolipidosis II, so enzyme mistargeting is incomplete and disease is milder and slower. Lysosomal hydrolases are partly secreted rather than delivered intracellularly, giving the same biochemical pattern of high plasma and low cellular enzyme activity, with gradual accumulation of undegraded substrate. The predominant clinical burden is on connective tissue and the skeleton. Inheritance is autosomal recessive.
additionalDifferentials: Mucolipidosis II (I-cell disease) at the severe end of the pathway
Attenuated mucopolysaccharidoses such as Scheie or Maroteaux-Lamy
Juvenile idiopathic arthritis given the joint stiffness
Multiple epiphyseal dysplasia and other skeletal dysplasias
Other lysosomal storage disorders with slowly progressive arthropathy
additionalInvestigations: Plasma or serum assay of multiple lysosomal enzymes showing raised activity
Cultured fibroblast studies demonstrating reduced intracellular enzyme activity
GNPTAB and GNPTG gene sequencing to define the subtype
Skeletal survey and hip imaging for dysplasia
redFlags: Marked functional decline from advancing joint contractures
reference.prognosis: The course is slowly progressive, and many patients survive into adulthood; the main long-term burden comes from joint contractures, hip disease, and cardiac valve involvement, which can cause significant disability.
pitfalls: Mistaking early joint stiffness for inflammatory arthritis and delaying metabolic diagnosis
Assuming normal intellect excludes a lysosomal disorder
Overlooking the diagnostic pattern of high plasma lysosomal enzyme activity
Failing to distinguish the milder ML III course from severe ML II
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
management: Supportive multidisciplinary care, as there is no enzyme-replacement or curative therapy for this disorder
Physiotherapy and occupational therapy to preserve joint mobility and slow the progression of contractures
Orthopaedic management of progressive hip and joint disease, including joint replacement in adulthood
Analgesia and mobility aids for joint pain and stiffness
Cardiac surveillance with periodic echocardiography for valvular involvement, with cardiology referral
Ophthalmology review for corneal changes, alongside regular skeletal monitoring
Genetic counselling and family screening for this autosomal recessive condition involving GNPTAB or GNPTG
